extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent litigators, and law students studying U.S. patent law
extracted.subtask_description: A compendium of doctrinal rules and practical criteria for patentability, claim/specification drafting, infringement, remedies, evidence, and procedural requirements under U.S. patent law as summarized in a legal treatise index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment by disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification may be amended by disclaimer; mode of amending imperfect specification by disclaimer; disclaimer merely strikes out what is disclaimed and cannot be read in explanation of what remains; when allowed and by whom to be made; enures to benefit of assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to narrow a patent's scope without adding matter; disclaimers cannot be used to interpret what remains; statutory allowance and timing important; assignees benefit from disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment by surrender and reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification may be amended by surrender and reissue; action of commissioner in granting reissue conclusive; reissue may give an invalid patent validity; right of reissue does not authorize surrender for fraudulent purposes; applies to extended patents; gives patentee power to retain whatever he deems proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue is formal mechanism to correct/amend patents but constrained by fraud doctrine and commissioner action; reissue may operate differently for extended terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application form and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Application for letters-patent in form of petition; verified by oath; if granted, valid although not verified; form of oath when varied; affirmation substituted for oath in statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oath/verification is usually required and is prima facie evidence of novelty, but irregularities may be cured by grant; procedural formalities matter but grant can cure some defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application completion/abandonment timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Application abandoned unless completed within two years (statutory reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely completion of an application is required to avoid abandonment; statutory deadlines govern prosecution timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be applicant/patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules identifying who may be applicant for letters-patent (statutory references); first inventor alone entitled to a patent; meaning of 'first inventor' under statute; patentee must believe himself to be first inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper identification of applicant is required; disputes (e.g., derivation, first-to-invent issues in older law) resolved by courts/statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim: object and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Object of the claim is not to aid the description but to ascertain what is claimed as new; claim is a means of clearly presenting the subject-matter of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims define the monopoly; drafter must focus claims on delimiting novel subject-matter rather than restating the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must distinguish old from new
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must distinguish between the old and the new; need not describe old in detail; not presumed to cover well-known articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be drafted to make the novel aspects clear; background does not need exhaustive description in the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim ambiguity rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous claims that cover a whole class of subjects of which only one answers are problematic; where each method answers, claim not ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drafting claims that overbroadly cover classes where only some members perform the invention; clarity prevents indefiniteness challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims and abstract principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must not be for an abstract principle; must be for a principle embodied in a particular organism/machine/method; claim for an abstract principle invalid because it prevents subsequent invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should recite concrete applications or structures; purely abstract claims are invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for machines vs processes/products
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim for a machine will not cover a process and vice versa; though clumsily worded a claim may cover both process and product in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafters must choose claim categories carefully; mixed drafting can create uncertainty as to scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to variations and combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for variations in application of a general principle must be drafted appropriately; for a combination, how claim scope is determined; for an applied principle, claims will cover similar methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming combinations or variant applications, specify the essential cooperative elements or the manner of application to bind equivalents as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim sufficiency and judicial construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficiency of claims is decided by the court; construction of patent/claim by court (and sometimes jury), judged liberally; principles of construction listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction doctrines matter heavily in litigation; courts construe claims in light of specification and prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification/Description statutory sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification sufficiency is required by statute; must be sufficient for persons skilled in the art; must enable skilled workmen to apply without further invention of their own; must not omit any step/process which facilitates the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement and written description doctrines require the disclosure to teach the invention to a person of ordinary skill; omissions of essential steps or ingredients can invalidate a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification need not explain well-known matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification need not explain what is well known; need not explain slight deviations; long and complicated processes construed liberally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not waste specification space on common general knowledge, but provide enough detail on the novel aspects and on non-obvious features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and drawings interplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings accompany specifications of machinery and form part of the specification; drawings and description are mutually explanatory; drawings ordinarily need not be made to scale; drawings attested by inventor and two witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings are part of the disclosure and can supply details omitted from the written description; proper attestation/formalities for drawings are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of essential elements fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission from the specification of what is essential is fatal; omission of an ingredient or step in a well-known process may in some cases be patentable if it affects degree of benefit only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the specification discloses all essential elements required for practicing the claimed invention; missing essentials can render the patent invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must disclose source/procurement of unusual ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must state where unusual ingredients may be procured and how to remove injurious foreign matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For chemical or biological inventions, disclose sources and purification/removal steps for non-standard reagents or materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of sufficiency and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of sufficiency of the specification and of utility must be offered by the patentee; evidence of utility is a factor in novelty inquiries; courts/juries decide utility questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to adduce experimental or expert evidence to show the invention works and is useful for its stated purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty statutory requisite and tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is a statutory requisite; novelty of a process/composition/machine determined by courts; not governed by fixed rules; failure of novelty renders patent void; amount of thought implied in novelty discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct thorough prior art searches; novelty can be defeated by prior publications, uses, or patents; jurisdictional differences (England vs US) noted regarding effect of parts lacking novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility as a patentability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility (useful) has two meanings: not injurious and capable of practical application; want of utility equivalent to want of novelty in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserted inventions must have practical utility and not be merely theoretical or injurious; utility may be part of novelty analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention sufficiency and frivolous inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficiency of invention discussed (what constitutes invention); frivolous inventions are not patentable; invention does not consist merely in use of cheaper materials; patentability decided by character of the result, not the amount of ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate a real, useful advance; mere cost savings or trivial changes without practical benefit may not support patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles/theories not patentable; application can be
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere principle or law of nature is not patentable; the requisites for patenting a 'principle' are discussed; a claim for an abstract principle is invalid; where an inventor describes a mode of application, applied principles may be patentable and will cover similar methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should recite practical application/implementation of underlying principles rather than claiming the principle itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process vs machine vs manufacture distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between machine, process, and manufacture; a process may be a manufacture under English interpretation; cannot claim a process as an improvement in machinery; processes and products may be claimed together when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose correct statutory category for the claim; statutory interpretation and precedent influence claim strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of ingredients test
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution of new for old ingredients in a process which produces a beneficial result is patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that substitution yields new, non-obvious, and beneficial results to support patentability of process changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical and chemical equivalents in infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement analysis involves doctrine of mechanical equivalents and chemical equivalents; mechanical equivalents are not confined to those strictly known as such in mechanics; jury to decide whether equivalents used; infringement by equivalents may occur even when equivalent is patentable per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing infringement, consider equivalence doctrine; slight structural changes that perform substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result may infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement: acts that constitute infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement consists in making, using, or vending; punishable by action at law; includes making patented machine, using patented process (subject to exceptions), and selling articles made by a patented machine in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze accused activity against each claim element; consider process, product, and machine claims separately and together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a patented machine for purposes of experiments may not be an infringement (quære); experiments/experimental use and their relation to abandonment and prior use discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited experimental uses may be defensible but are fact-specific; courts examine intent and commercial nature of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of materials and articles produced by patented machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale of the materials of a patented machine is not per se an infringement; sale of articles produced by a patented machine is not necessarily an infringement; whether product sale infringes depends on claim coverage (process vs product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on claim scope: if patent claims the product, sale may infringe; if only the machine is claimed, sale of products may not infringe absent process/product claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidental production and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidental production of a patented article in the course of a different activity may not per se constitute infringement; incidental use of patented process for a different purpose may not be infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the production/use was intentionally part of the accused infringing activity or merely incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of combination claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement of a combination claim depends on whether the accused device or process practices the combination; may turn upon use of equivalents; where parts of a combination are novel, the combination may be infringed even if components individually differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence of all claim elements or their equivalents; missing an essential cooperative element may avoid infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial identity and manufacture infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement of a manufacture is a question of substantial identity; identity of two machines or improvements explained generally and cannot be decided by fixed rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for practical and substantial identity rather than literal identity; courts consider overall function and result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions and essential ingredients in process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the proportions of ingredients are essential, there is no infringement to vary them; varying essential proportions may avoid infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that specify critical proportions can limit scope; accused products with materially different proportions may avoid infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of utility as infringement test
rubrics_metrics.description: Superior utility of an accused product may be a test in infringement analysis (i.e., practical and substantial identity may consider relative utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may consider differences in utility when weighing identity/equivalence; improved function can be dispositive in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages are actual, not vindictive; may be trebled by the court; are the amount of profits actually made by defendant (not hypothetical profits); include losses suffered by patentee through piracy; must be calculated, not guessed at; nominal damages available where only making is proved; do not include counsel fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of damages requires accounting and evidence of actual profits attributable to infringement; treble damages may attach for willful infringement but counsel fees generally not recoverable as damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable remedies—injunction standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts of equity may restrain infringements by injunction; injunctions are governed by general equitable principles: bill should contain particulars and be sworn to; injunctions denied in cases of abandonment or laches; notice must be served on defendant; injunctions are always special; indemnity orders not usual; injunctions considered before and after trial with rules and tests for granting (three classes of cases, full hearing, effect on defendant's business, novelty issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek injunctions when equitable balance favors patentee; equitable defenses (laches, acquiescence) can bar relief; courts weigh hardship, public interest, and validity/novelty disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of profits and inspection in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity courts may order account of profits and mutual inspection; account of profits ordered in certain cases and what comprised under account discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable relief can include monetary accounting and discovery measures; patentee should plead and prove basis for accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of use, identity, novelty, sufficiency, and utility: two kinds of evidence in patent cause; prima facie evidence of novelty and invention; burden of proof rules (defendant to show lack of novelty; patentee to show infringement and sufficiency); plaintiff's own declarations inadmissible after assignment; expert testimony rules; who may be experts; admissibility and weight of experts; expert evidence for defendant must be positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop factual and expert record: witnesses competent to the subject-matter, credible positive defenses, and admissible technical proof; jury vs court roles established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts: competence and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony used where resorted to; who regarded as experts depends on subject-matter; practical workmen may serve as experts; experts admissible to prove facts and give opinions; experts to be submitted to jury under proper instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose experts with appropriate technical credentials and practical experience; courts evaluate credibility and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use and printed publication as novelty destroyers
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior public use destroys right to a patent; meaning of public use and its timing discussed; prior description in a public work inconsistent with novelty; printed publications and public works defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and analyze any prior public use/publication that predates application; consider geographic/foreign differences in prior use effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior experiments and lost arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Antecedent experiments by others may be used by an inventor; experiments distinguished from invention; invention may be discoverer of a lost art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental activity by earlier actors may or may not negate novelty depending on completeness, abandonment, and public nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat protection for incomplete inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveat protects incomplete inventions; caveat for an incomplete invention is not conclusive evidence of incompleteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a caveat may provide provisional protection, but it does not itself decide novelty or completeness issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment formalities and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment before letters-patent confers an inchoate right; assignment of an incomplete invention is only valid as a contract; legal formalities of assignments; whether a particular instrument amounts to assignment; assignment after letters-patent regulated by statute; recording clauses interpretation; unrecorded assignments good except against purchasers for value in good faith; assignment implies no warranty of title; assignment of part of patent constitutes joint ownership; agreement to convey future term is not an assignment; presumption that nothing but present term assigned; assignment by operation of law (bankruptcy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe statutory recording requirements and drafting clarity; purchasers and creditors may have priority depending on recording and good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignee rights unaffected by a reissue; entitled to benefit of disclaimer; rights under extension or renewal; rights where term extended by special enactment; assignee may apply for patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignee's proprietary rights are robust but may be affected by certain post-issuance proceedings and statutory mechanisms for term extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee position and estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between licensee and assignee; licensee estopped to some extent; cannot recover royalties paid; whether he can withhold payments after patent declared invalid examined; those who continue to use may be estopped; licensee remedies under agreement violation discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License agreements should allocate risk for validity rulings and royalty disputes; continuing to use post-invalidity can create estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction of Congress and federal courts; original jurisdiction of Circuit and District Courts, appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court; federal courts' exclusive jurisdiction and limitations (e.g., contracts under patent not per se federal); in what judicial district a suit must be brought; jurisdiction of the person allows injunctive relief in other districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose forum and venue consistent with statutory jurisdictional rules; personal jurisdiction affects injunctive reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court vs jury roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Court's province to construe letters-patent and decide whether claims are explicit; jury to pass on use of mechanical equivalents, novelty, sufficiency of specification (under proper instructions), and questions of infringement and utility in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigation strategy must account for mixed questions of law and fact; prepare for claim construction hearings and jury trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue: when allowed and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue allowed to correct defects; new patent issued on surrender of the old; presumed to be for same invention; action of commissioner in granting reissue conclusive; when allowed and the effect on assignees and pending suits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reissue to correct clear errors but be mindful of estoppel, fraud risks, and potential impact on existing litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension and renewal of patent term
rubrics_metrics.description: Extension of patent term: when and by whom granted historically; action of commissioner in granting extension not re-examinable; now must be by special act; term virtually extended to certain years; does not destroy right to use a lawfully acquired patented machine during extension; rights of assignees under extension; specification may be surrendered and reissued during an extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term extensions are extraordinary, statutory matters; check applicable statutes and legislative acts for extension rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repair doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawful owner of a patented machine may repair it; repair distinguished from reconstruction which may be infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners may maintain/repair devices to preserve utility; complete reconstruction to create a new article may infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks and statutory labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks required to be put on patented articles for sale (statutory reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with marking statutes to preserve right to damages for unmarked infringement periods and to provide public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Burden of proof: on defendant to show want of novelty; on patentee to show infringement and sufficiency of specification; when burden shifts noted (e.g., on patentee in certain situations); evidence of novelty, invention and utility discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare to shoulder or rebut burdens of proof with appropriate evidence and expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repugnancy between title and description
rubrics_metrics.description: Repugnancy between the title of the patent and the description of the specification is fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistency between the claim/title and the specification to avoid invalidity for repugnancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptions from patent grant
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent itself is evidence of novelty; new patent issued on surrender presumed to be for the same invention; action of commissioner may be conclusive in some respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent grant creates prima facie presumptions but can be rebutted by evidence of prior art or fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of damages must be direct and calculated
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of damages must be directly to the point and calculated, not guessed at; general rule for estimating damages provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare accounting and direct evidence tying defendant's profits/losses to the infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention relevant to abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Intention may be material to show abandonment; abandonment and intent discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inventor's conduct and intent when evaluating whether a prior public use or abandonment bars patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability of vendors and contractors
rubrics_metrics.description: One contracting for articles to be made by a patented machine may be an infringer; vendor of articles made by patented machines may be responsible if connected with use of the machine; sale of materials of a patented machine not per se infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider secondary liability theories for parties who induce or contribute to infringing manufacture or sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity consequences of fraudulent procurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraud in obtaining a reissue or in procurement of the patent vitiates letters-patent and renders patent invalidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure candor and good faith in prosecution and reissue to avoid invalidity for fraud/concealment.
